mainTopic: Losing a claim by making a field a boundary marker, the lost path to a field, and a palm tree left to a daughter
overview: This amud opens by finishing a point about documents: judges may sign one without reading it, because they only confirm the witnesses' signatures. Next comes the משנה's case of someone who described a field as another person's by using it as a boundary marker (סימן). אביי says he loses his claim only if he wrote this in someone else's document. If he wrote it in his own purchase deed, he can say the seller would not have sold otherwise, and he could not make a secret protest (מודעא), since secrets spread. In a real case, אביי first rules that the man lost his claim. The orphans' steward then wins back the field with two claims from רבי יוחנן: 'I marked only one furrow' and 'I bought it back.' A new משנה follows about a man whose path to his field was lost. אדמון lets him take the shortest route, while חכמים say he must buy a path, and רב and רבא explain when they disagree. The amud ends with two cases of a father who left 'a palm tree' to his daughter. In one, the heirs must give her a tree and divide the estate again. In the other, two half-trees count as 'a palm tree.'

steps.title: Judges may sign without reading the document
steps.stepSummary: Unlike witnesses, judges may sign a document even if they did not read it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But judges may sign even though they did not read it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an earlier point. Witnesses should read a document before signing it, but judges may sign it without reading it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses sign to confirm what the document says, so they must know what it says. Judges only confirm that the witnesses' signatures are real. They are not confirming the content, so they do not need to read it.
steps.confusionAlert: The judges' signature here only confirms the witnesses' signatures. It says nothing about what the document itself says.

phrases.english: But the judges sign
even though they did not read it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion about witnesses signing documents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judges may sign a document without reading it, because they only confirm the signatures.

steps.title: אביי limits the boundary-marker rule to a document for someone else
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that someone who used a field as a boundary marker for another field loses his claim to it. אביי says this applies only in a document written for another person, not in his own purchase.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If he made it a marker for another.' אביי said: This was taught only when it was for another person. But if it was for himself, he did not lose his right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of using a field as a סימן. Then אביי narrows it: the man loses his right only if he wrote this in someone else's document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling a field 'Reuven's field' as the border of another field sounds like admitting Reuven owns it. אביי says that admission counts only when nothing pushed him to make it. If he wrote it in his own purchase deed, he keeps his claim, and the next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: A marker, here a boundary marker in a document
He lost his right (to claim the field)
They taught this only in the case of

phrases.english: He made it a marker for another.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: he described the disputed field as someone else's when marking the border of a different field.

phrases.english: אביי said:
They taught this only about another person,
but for himself,
he did not lose his right.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לְאַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using a field as a סימן loses a person's claim only in another person's document, not in his own purchase.

steps.title: Why the buyer keeps his claim
steps.stepSummary: The buyer can say: if I had not written it that way, the seller would not have sold to me.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say: 'If I had not done this for him, he would not have sold it to me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains אביי's reason. The buyer only wrote the field as the seller's in order to get the sale done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller holds the disputed field and is also selling the buyer a neighboring field. If the buyer had refused to call the disputed field the seller's, the seller would have walked away. So writing it that way was not a real admission.

phrases.english: Because he can say:
If I had not done this for him,
he would not have sold it to me,

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר: אִי דְּלָא עֲבַדִי לֵיהּ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for אביי's limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A statement made under pressure to close a purchase is not a real admission.

steps.title: Should he have made a secret protest?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a possible objection: the buyer should have made a מודעא, a protest before witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: What can you say? 'I should have made a protest before witnesses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא imagines someone arguing against the buyer: if you were forced, you should have told witnesses ahead of time that you did not mean it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, someone who acts under pressure protects himself with a מודעא, a statement before witnesses that his act is not sincere. Since this buyer made no such protest, it looks as if he meant what he wrote. This sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A protest declared before witnesses ahead of time
To hand over, here to make (a protest)

phrases.english: What can you say?
That I should have made a protest?
phrases.notes: The buyer is putting the other side's argument into words so he can answer it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִית לָךְ לְמֵימַר? אִיבְּעִי לִי לְמִימְסַר מוֹדָעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a possible weak spot in the buyer's argument.
steps.kashyaTarget: The buyer's claim that he was forced to write the field as the seller's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone acting under pressure should have made a מודעא, and he did not.

steps.title: Secrets always spread
steps.stepSummary: The buyer answers that a protest would have leaked to the seller, and the sale would have fallen through.
steps.simpleTranslation: Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The buyer answers the objection. A protest before witnesses would not stay secret, so making one would have ruined the deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word would pass from one friend to the next until it reached the seller. Then the seller would refuse to sell. So not making a מודעא does not weaken the buyer's claim, and אביי's rule stands.
steps.whatToRemember: In his own purchase deed, a buyer who calls a field the seller's keeps his claim. He was pressured, and he could not safely make a secret protest.

phrases.english: your friend has a friend,
and your friend's friend has a friend.
phrases.notes: In other words, the protest would have spread until the seller heard about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection about the מודעא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning: a protest was not possible without ruining the deal.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Not making a מודעא shows he truly admitted the field was the seller's.
steps.terutzMaskana: A protest would have leaked, so his silence is excused and he keeps his claim.

steps.title: אביי rules on a real case: the man lost his right
steps.stepSummary: A man made a field a marker for another, later claimed it, and died. His steward came before אביי, who ruled that the man had lost his right.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who made a field a marker for another, then claimed it, and died, after appointing a steward. The steward came before אביי. אביי told him: 'He made it a marker for another, so he lost his right.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case. אביי applies the משנה's rule and rules against the man's estate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the marker was written for another person, not in the man's own purchase. So the exception from step 2 does not help, and אביי's first ruling is that the claim is lost. In the next steps the steward finds arguments that limit this loss.

keyTerms.meaning: A steward who manages property for others, here for orphans

phrases.english: There was a certain man who made it a marker for another,
he contested it, and died,
and he had appointed a steward.
The steward came before אביי.
He said to him:
He made it a marker for another,
he lost his right.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies אביי's rule from step 2 to a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who made a field a marker for another person has lost his claim to it.

steps.title: The steward argues the father marked only one furrow
steps.stepSummary: The steward argues that the father, if alive, would have said he used only one furrow of the field as the boundary marker, not the whole field.
steps.simpleTranslation: The steward said: If the orphans' father were alive, he would have claimed: 'I made only one furrow as a marker for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The steward pushes back against אביי's ruling. He offers an argument the dead father could have made for himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי had ruled that marking the field as a boundary means the father lost his claim to it. The steward narrows that loss. He says the boundary was only one strip at the edge of the field, so only that strip is lost and the rest belongs to the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: would claim, would argue in court
a furrow, a plowed strip of a field

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: אִי הֲוָה אֲבוּהוֹן דְּיַתְמֵי קַיָּים,
phrases.english: He said: If the father of the orphans were alive,
phrases.notes: "He" is the steward from the story in step 6.

phrases.english: he would have claimed and said:
'I made one furrow for you.'
phrases.notes: He means only one strip at the edge of the field served as the boundary marker, not the whole field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הֲוָה אֲבוּהוֹן דְּיַתְמֵי קַיָּים, הֲוָה טָעֵין וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to אביי's ruling in step 6 by arguing for a narrower loss.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the loss
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole field is lost because it was used as a boundary marker.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only one furrow was meant as the marker, so only that strip is lost.

steps.title: אביי accepts the one-furrow argument
steps.stepSummary: אביי agrees, citing רבי יוחנן's ruling that this claim is believed, and orders the steward to give the other side just one furrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: You have spoken well. רבי יוחנן said that if someone claims 'I made one furrow for you,' he is believed. Go and give him at least one furrow.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי accepts the steward's argument. He backs it up with a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן rules that a person who claims he marked only one furrow is believed. A court may raise this claim on behalf of orphans who cannot argue for themselves. So the other side receives only the single furrow, and the rest of the field stays with the orphans.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have spoken well.
For Rabbi Yochanan said,
If he claimed and said,
'I made one furrow for you,' he is believed.

phrases.aramaic: זִיל הַב לֵיהּ מִיהַת תֶּלֶם אֶחָד.
phrases.english: Go, give him at least one furrow.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the other side, the person the father had named as the field's owner in the boundary marker.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Approves the steward's claim from step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That the one-furrow claim is accepted
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling that this claim is believed

steps.title: The steward argues the father bought the furrow back
steps.stepSummary: The one furrow had a row of palm trees on it. The steward argues that the father would have claimed he later bought it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: On that furrow there was a row of palm trees. The steward said: If the orphans' father were alive, he would have claimed: 'I went back and bought it from him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The steward does not want to lose the valuable palm trees on that furrow. So he makes a second argument for the orphans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steward now admits the furrow did belong to the other side. But he claims the father bought it back later. If that is believed, even this one furrow stays with the orphans.

phrases.english: There was on it a row of palm trees,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי הֲוָה אֲבוּהוֹן דְּיַתְמֵי קַיָּים,
phrases.english: He said to him: If the father of the orphans were alive,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה טָעֵין וְאָמַר, חָזַרְתִּי וְלָקַחְתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ.
phrases.english: he would have claimed and said: I went back and bought it from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the outcome of step 8, which gave away one furrow.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New factual claim on the orphans' behalf
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The furrow with the palm trees goes to the other side.
steps.terutzMaskana: The father bought the furrow back, so it belongs to the orphans.

steps.title: אביי accepts the bought-back argument
steps.stepSummary: אביי agrees again, citing רבי יוחנן's ruling that the claim 'I went back and bought it' is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: You have spoken well. רבי יוחנן said that if someone claims 'I went back and bought it from him,' he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי accepts the second argument too, again relying on רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן rules that a person who claims he bought the land back is believed. Since the court raises this claim for the orphans, the furrow with the palm trees stays with them as well.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have spoken well.
For Rabbi Yochanan said:
If he claimed and said,
'I went back and bought it from him,' he is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Approves the steward's second claim from step 9.
steps.raayaObject: That the bought-back claim is accepted
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling that this claim is believed

steps.title: אביי praises the steward as a model
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that anyone appointing a steward should choose someone like this, who knows how to argue for the orphans' rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Whoever appoints a steward should appoint someone like this, who knows how to turn things toward the orphans' rights.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with אביי's lesson about the kind of steward people should appoint.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steward turned a full loss into a full win by finding valid claims the father could have made. אביי holds this up as the ideal. A good steward actively searches for every legitimate argument on the orphans' behalf.

keyTerms.meaning: a steward or guardian over someone's property
to turn things over in favor of (someone's) rights

steps.whatToRemember: A court and a steward may raise claims the dead father could have made. Two of רבי יוחנן's rulings ('one furrow' and 'I bought it back') saved the whole field for the orphans.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
One who appoints a steward,
should appoint one like this,
who knows how to turn things toward the rights of orphans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story with a general lesson.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A good steward finds every valid argument that protects the orphans.

steps.title: The lost path to a field: אדמון and חכמים disagree
steps.stepSummary: A man went overseas and the path to his field was lost. אדמון says he may take the shortest route. חכמים say he must buy a path, however expensive, or fly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone went overseas and the path to his field was lost, אדמון says: let him take the shortest route. חכמים say: let him buy a path even for a hundred מנה, or fly through the air.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It presents a disagreement about a person whose path to his field can no longer be identified.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אדמון holds that the owner still has a right of way, so he may use the shortest route to his field. חכמים hold that he has no automatic right. He must buy a path, and 'fly through the air' is their sharp way of saying nobody owes him one.

keyTerms.meaning: a large coin, worth one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who went overseas
and the path to his field was lost.
Admon says: Let him go by the shortest route.

phrases.aramaic: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: יִקְנֶה לוֹ דֶּרֶךְ בְּמֵאָה מָנֶה,
phrases.english: And the Rabbis say: Let him buy himself a path for a hundred maneh,
phrases.notes: This means at whatever price the neighbor asks, even a huge one.

phrases.english: or let him fly through the air.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic with a new משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדמון: shortest route. חכמים: he must buy a path.

steps.title: Why do חכמים disagree with אדמון?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges חכמים: אדמון seems clearly right, since the man definitely had a path.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of חכמים? אדמון is speaking well!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by questioning חכמים, since אדמון's view seems obviously correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the man owned a path through the neighbor's land. So why should he lose it just because its exact spot is forgotten? The neighbor should at least give him the shortest route.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason of the Rabbis?
Admon speaks well!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְרַבָּנַן, שַׁפִּיר קָאָמַר אַדְמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the view of חכמים in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The man had a path for sure, so the neighbor should owe him at least the shortest route.

steps.title: רב: the field is surrounded by four different owners
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the case is a field surrounded on all four sides by four different people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The case is where four people surround the field on its four sides.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question by defining the case more precisely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If four different neighbors surround the field, each one can say, 'The path was not through my land.' The owner cannot prove which neighbor owes him the path. That is why חכמים say he must buy one.
steps.confusionAlert: חכמים do not deny that the man once had a path. Their point is that he cannot prove which neighbor's land it crossed.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
For example, where four people surrounded it
on its four sides.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There is one neighbor who clearly owes the path.
steps.terutzMaskana: Four different neighbors surround the field, so none of them can be forced to give the path.

steps.title: Then what is אדמון's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks: if four different people surround the field, why does אדמון let him take the shortest route?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the reason of אדמון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the question around and now challenges אדמון. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With four separate neighbors, each can push the man away from his own land. So it is now hard to see how אדמון can force any of them to give the shortest route.

phrases.english: If so, what is the reason of Admon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב's explanation in step 14 to challenge the other side of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If each of the four neighbors can deny the path ran through his land, no one can be forced to give the shortest route.

steps.title: רבא narrows the dispute to one owner who bought from four
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that with four separate owners, everyone agrees the claimant can be pushed off. The argument is only when one person bought all four fields from four different sellers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If four owners got their fields from four sellers, or four owners got their fields from one seller, everyone agrees each owner can push the claimant away. The argument is when one owner got all four fields from four sellers.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from step 15: why would אדמון let him take the shortest route if four different people surround the field? He says אדמון doesn't say that in such a case at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If four separate people own the fields, each one can say 'your path wasn't through my land,' so no single owner can be forced to give a path. The real argument is when one person now owns all four fields, but bought them from four different sellers. Then the path is surely somewhere on his land, but he can still point back to the original sellers.

keyTerms.meaning: by the power of; getting your rights from someone else, such as a seller
push him off, turn away his claim

steps.confusionAlert: Even 'four owners who came from one seller' counts as a case where everyone agrees. Each of the four current owners can still say the path wasn't on his piece.

phrases.english: Rava said:
In a case of four owners who come by the power of four,
phrases.notes: Four current owners, each of whom bought his field from a different seller.

phrases.english: and four owners who come by the power of one
everyone agrees
that he can push him off.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּחַד דְּאָתֵי מִכֹּחַ אַרְבְּעָה.
phrases.english: Where they argue is one owner who comes by the power of four.
phrases.notes: One person bought all four surrounding fields from four different sellers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: בְּאַרְבְּעָה דְּאָתוּ מִכֹּחַ אַרְבְּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 by changing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought אדמון lets him take the shortest route even when four separate people surround the field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is only when one owner bought all four fields from four sellers. With four separate owners, everyone agrees he can be pushed off.

steps.title: The reasoning of אדמון and חכמים
steps.stepSummary: אדמון says the path is surely on the buyer's land. חכמים say the buyer can threaten to return the deeds to the original sellers, and then the claimant cannot sue anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: אדמון holds the claimant can say: Either way, I have a path through your land. חכמים hold the owner can say: If you keep quiet and settle, fine. If not, I'll give the deeds back to the original sellers, and you won't be able to bring a case against them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא now explains why each side rules the way it does in the case of one buyer from four sellers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אדמון, since one person owns all the land around, the path must be somewhere on it, so he gives the shortest route. For חכמים, the buyer can hand each deed back to its original seller. Then the claimant faces four separate people again, each able to push him off, so he has no real power and must buy a path.
steps.whatToRemember: With one buyer from four sellers: אדמון says 'the path is surely on your land,' and חכמים say 'I can send you back to four separate sellers.'

phrases.english: Admon holds:

phrases.aramaic: מִכׇּל מָקוֹם דַּרְכָּא אִית לִי גַּבָּךְ.
phrases.english: In any case, I have a path on your land.
And the Rabbis hold:
If you keep quiet, keep quiet,
phrases.notes: The owner means: if you accept a settlement quietly, fine.

phrases.english: and if not
I will return the deeds to their owners
and you will not be able to bring a case against them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְמוֹן סָבַר: מִכׇּל מָקוֹם דַּרְכָּא אִית לִי גַּבָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבא's case in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the reasoning of each side
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since one owner holds all the land, it seemed the claimant must win.
steps.terutzMaskana: חכמים allow the owner to send the claimant back to the four original sellers, so the claimant loses his advantage.

steps.title: A palm tree left to a daughter
steps.stepSummary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter in his will. The sons divided the estate and gave her no tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his heirs: A palm tree for my daughter. The orphans went and divided the property, and they didn't give her a palm tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story that it will compare to the path case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father did not say which palm tree. After the sons split the land, each son can claim the daughter's tree isn't in his share, just as each field owner could say the path wasn't on his land.

keyTerms.meaning: orphans, here meaning the sons who inherited

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to them:
A palm tree for my daughter.
The orphans went and divided the property,
they did not give her a palm tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case, which will be compared to the path case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the daughter was left an unspecified palm tree, and the sons divided the estate without giving her one.

steps.title: רב יוסף compares it to the path case
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף thought this case is the same as the path case in the משנה, so each son could push her off.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף thought to say: This is the same as our משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף wants to decide the palm tree case by comparing it to the משנה about the lost path.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as each field owner can say 'the path wasn't on my land,' each son could say 'your tree isn't in my share.' That would leave the daughter with nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: he thought to say; a first idea that is often rejected
this is the same as our משנה

phrases.english: Rav Yosef thought to say:
This is our mishna.
phrases.notes: He means the משנה about the man whose path to his field was lost (step 12).

steps.triggerLanguage: סְבַר רַב יוֹסֵף לְמֵימַר: הַיְינוּ מַתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to decide the case from step 18 using the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That the sons can each push off the daughter's claim.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the lost path, where each surrounding owner can push off the claimant.

steps.title: אביי: the cases are not alike
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects the comparison. In the path case, each owner can truly say the path wasn't his. Here, the palm tree is owed by all the sons together.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Are they really the same? There, each owner can push him off. Here, the palm tree is with them.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי knocks down רב יוסף's comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the path case, each owner may really be innocent, since the path might never have crossed his field. Here, the tree came from the estate the sons all shared before they divided it. So the debt belongs to all of them together, and none of them can escape it.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Are they comparable?
There, each and every one
can push him off,
here, the palm tree is with them.
phrases.notes: The tree came out of the estate they all inherited together, so they all hold it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison made in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole comparison between the palm tree case and the path case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In the path case, each owner may truly not owe anything. In the palm tree case, the sons owe the tree together from the shared estate.

steps.title: The fix: give her the tree and divide again
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the sons must give the daughter a palm tree and then divide the estate again from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is their fix? They should give her a palm tree, and then go back and divide the property again from the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי closes the case by telling the sons what to do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the tree from one son's share would make him lose more than his brothers. So after the daughter gets her tree, the sons divide the rest of the estate again, and everyone shares the loss equally.
steps.whatToRemember: A tree left to the daughter is owed by all the heirs together. They give her a tree and then divide the estate again from the start.

phrases.english: What is their fix?
Let them give her a palm tree
and go back and divide from the beginning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on אביי's point in step 20 and gives the practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The sons must give the daughter a palm tree and then divide the estate again from the start.

steps.title: A father leaves 'a palm tree' to his daughter but owns only two half-trees
steps.stepSummary: A man said in his will, 'A palm tree for my daughter.' When he died, he owned no whole tree, only two halves of palm trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who told his family, 'Give a palm tree to my daughter.' He died and left only two halves of palm trees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a new case that is similar to the one before it. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case the sons gave the daughter nothing. Here the father owned no whole tree at all, only half of one tree and half of another. So the question is whether those two halves can count as the 'palm tree' he promised her.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to them:
A palm tree for my daughter.
He died and left behind
two halves of palm trees.
phrases.notes: He owned half of one tree and half of another, not one whole tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case about the same kind of will as step 18, with a new detail: the father owned only half-trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets out the case. The father promised a palm tree, but his estate holds only two halves of palm trees.

steps.title: רב אשי asks whether two half-trees are called 'a palm tree'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי was unsure whether, in everyday speech, two halves of palm trees are called 'a palm tree.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי sat and was bothered by this: Do people call two halves of palm trees 'a palm tree,' or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks a question about how people normally talk. The answer will decide what the father meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A will is read the way regular people speak. If people call two half-trees 'a palm tree,' then the heirs can give her the two halves. If they don't, the father meant a whole tree.

keyTerms.meaning: It was difficult for him; he was unsure

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ' with a קשיא that attacks someone's view. Here it just means רב אשי was unsure and asked a real question.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi sat
and it was difficult for him:
Do people call
two halves of palm trees
'a palm tree,' or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב אָשֵׁי וְקָא קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to read the father's words from step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, in normal speech, two half palm trees count as 'a palm tree.'

steps.title: רב מרדכי quotes רבא: two half-trees are called 'a palm tree'
steps.stepSummary: רב מרדכי tells רב אשי a teaching from רבא, passed on by אבימי מהגרוניא: people do call two half-trees 'a palm tree.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרדכי said to רב אשי: אבימי from הגרוניא said this in the name of רבא: People do call two halves of palm trees 'a palm tree.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרדכי answers רב אשי's question with a teaching passed down from רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer is yes: in normal speech, two halves count as 'a palm tree.' So the father's words can mean these two halves, and the heirs can give her the halves he left. They do not need to give her a whole tree.

keyTerms.meaning: אבימי from the town of הגרוניא, who passed on רבא's teaching

steps.whatToRemember: A will is read the way people normally talk. Since people call two half-trees 'a palm tree,' the daughter can be given the two halves.
steps.whyThisMatters: Compare step 21. There the sons had to give the daughter a tree, because they had given her nothing. Here the halves already count as 'a palm tree,' so giving her them fulfills the father's words.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai said to Rav Ashi:
So said Avimi of Hagronya
in the name of Rava:
People do call
two halves of palm trees 'a palm tree.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי הָכִי אָמַר אֲבִימִי מֵהַגְרוֹנְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's question from step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. People call two halves of palm trees 'a palm tree,' so the two halves fulfill the father's words.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The heirs may give the daughter the two half-trees, because in normal speech they count as 'a palm tree.'
